is drawn with continuous motion along the entire length *Aa*; then the trapezoid described from that motion, or the rectangle *Aa* multiplied by 1/2 *aB* <note>original: "Aa x 1/2 aB"</note> which is equal to it, will be equal to the sum of all *MN* multiplied by *CM*, and therefore to the sum of all *Dd* multiplied by *DK*, which is the area *BKVT a*. This was to be demonstrated.

*Corollary.* From this, given the law of resistance and the difference *Aa* of the arcs *Ca* and *CB*, the proportion of the resistance to gravity can be gathered very nearly.

For if the resistance *DK* is uniform, the figure *BKTa* will be a rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*; and then the rectangle under 1/2 *Ba* and *Aa* will be equal to the rectangle under *Ba* and *DK*, and *DK* will be equal to 1/2 *Aa*. Therefore, since *DK* is the exponent <note>A mathematical representation of the magnitude of a force.</note> of the resistance, and the length of the pendulum is the exponent of gravity, the resistance will be to gravity as 1/2 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum; exactly as was demonstrated in proposition 28.

If the resistance is as the velocity, the figure *BKTa* will be an ellipsis very nearly. For if a body, in a non-resisting medium, should describe the length *BA* in a complete oscillation, the velocity in any place *D* would be as the ordinate *DE* of a circle described with diameter *AB*. Accordingly, since *Ba* in a resisting medium, and *BA* in a non-resisting medium, are described in approximately equal times; and therefore the velocities at each individual point of *Ba* are very nearly to the velocities at the corresponding points of the length *BA* as *Ba* is to *BA*; the velocity at point *D* in a resisting medium will be as the ordinate of a circle or ellipsis described upon the diameter *Ba*; and therefore the figure *BKVT a* will be an ellipsis very nearly. Since the resistance is supposed proportional to the velocity, let *OV* be the exponent of the resistance at the middle point *O*; and the ellipsis *BRVSa*, described with center *O* and semi-axes *OB*, *OV*, will be very nearly equal to the figure *BKVT a* and the rectangle *Aa* multiplied by *BO* equal to it. Therefore *Aa* multiplied by *BO* is to *OV* multiplied by *BO* as the area of this ellipsis is to *OV* multiplied by *BO*: that is, *Aa* is to *OV* as the area of a semi-circle is to the square of the radius, or as 11 to 7 approximately. And for that reason, 7/11 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum as the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity.

But if the resistance *DK* is in the duplicate ratio <note>The square of the ratio; resistance proportional to the square of the velocity.</note> of the velocity, the figure *BKVT a* will be almost a parabola having its vertex at *V* and axis *OV*, and therefore will be very nearly equal to the rectangle under 2/3 *Ba* and *OV*. Therefore the rectangle under 1/2 *Ba* and *Aa* is equal to the rectangle under 2/3 *Ba* and *OV*, and thus *OV* is equal to 3/4 *Aa*: and for that reason the resistance of the oscillating body at *O* is to its gravity as 3/4 *Aa* is to the length of the pendulum.

<summary>Newton establishes three corollaries for determining the ratio of resistance to gravity in a pendulum's motion, covering cases where resistance is constant, proportional to velocity, or proportional to the square of velocity.</summary>
